8h0s3ttbkp Tax or quota, when nobody knows the cost of abating

1prw0o30igc The state must choose its instrument before knowing how much it will cost the plants to cut their emissions. With a tax, it sets the price of polluting: each plant reduces until the next tonne costs it as much as the tax, so the quantity of emissions depends on its true cost. With a quota, it sets the quantity: emissions are known, but the cost of getting there is not. If each excess tonne does damage that climbs very fast, getting the quantity wrong is expensive: the quota protects better.

yai546zvjc Instrument choice under uncertainty ("prices versus quantities"): with a very steep [[MEC]] and an uncertain [[MAC]], a tax's quantity error creates a large loss; the quota fixes e and limits that loss. If MEC is flat and MAC steep, it's the reverse: the tax avoids excessive compliance costs. This is an argument about relative slopes, not a general rule.
aahl2scaon A tax guarantees the price of an avoided tonne, not the number of tonnes: if abating costs more than expected, the plants pollute more.
enwa6hu67n A quota guarantees the number of tonnes, not the cost: if abating costs more than expected, the plants pay a lot to meet the cap.
a0b5twhfg9 Which of the two errors costs more depends on the slopes: when marginal damage climbs fast, each excess tonne is very costly, so fixing the quantity is preferable.
